title: Turnus intra muros
titleEn: Turnus Inside the Walls — Aeneid IX.717–818
source: P. Vergilius Maro, Aeneid, ed. J. B. Greenough, The Bucolics, Aeneid, and Georgics of Virgil (Boston: Ginn & Company, 1881), public domain; TEI from PerseusDL/canonical-latinLit phi0690.phi003.perseus-lat2, sha256 e639e6a0e27427ef. Collated against The Latin Library (cltk mirror) as a disagreement detector only. Greenough's spelling kept (volnus, divom, Karthago, -is accusatives); his quotation marks printed as “ ”. Pronunciation convention: reconstructed Classical (restored) Latin, applied consistently. All translations were made fresh from the Latin for Lectorium.
about: The last stretch of Book IX. Mars puts heart into the Latins and sends Rout and Fear among the Trojans. Pandarus, seeing his brother Bitias dead in the gateway, heaves the gate shut on its hinges, leaving many of his own men outside; but in his haste he has shut Turnus in with him, like a tiger among helpless cattle. Turnus's armour flashes, the Trojans know the hated face, and Pandarus, burning to avenge his brother, tells him that this is no palace of Amata and no Ardea: he is in an enemy camp and will not get out. Turnus, smiling, tells him he will be able to report to Priam that a new Achilles has been found here. Juno turns Pandarus's spear aside, and Turnus splits his head in two with his sword. Had Turnus thought at once of breaking the bars and letting his army in, the war and the Trojan nation would have ended that day; instead his fury drives him on to kill man after man. At last Mnestheus and Serestus rally the fleeing Trojans with a speech of shame, and they press Turnus back towards the river, as hunters press a lion that will neither run nor charge. Jupiter sends Iris to forbid Juno to help him further. Under a storm of spears, his helmet ringing, his plumes struck away, streaming with sweat and gasping for breath, Turnus finally leaps in full armour into the Tiber, which bears him up on its waves and returns him, washed of the slaughter, to his friends.

sentences.t:
Hic Mars armipotens animum viresque Latinis
addidit et stimulos acris sub pectore vertit
immisitque Fugam Teucris atrumque Timorem.
sentences.l:
Here Mars, mighty in arms, courage and strength to the Latins
added, and goads keen beneath their breasts he plied,
and sent among the Teucrians Rout, and black Fear.
sentences.i: At this point Mars, the lord of arms, gave the Latins fresh courage and strength, worked sharp goads deep in their hearts, and let loose Rout and black Fear upon the Trojans.
sentences.n: A new paragraph in Greenough. 'Hic', 'here', at this moment, after Bitias's fall. 'armipotens', 'mighty in arms', a compound epithet of the epic kind. 'animum viresque', 'spirit and strength', the gifts of the war-god. 'stimulos acris', 'sharp goads', 'acris' accusative plural in '-is'; 'sub pectore vertit', 'turned (them) beneath the breast', plied them in their hearts. 'Fugam… Timorem', Rout and Fear as persons: in Homer Ares goes into battle with Deimos and Phobos, Terror and Rout, his attendants (Iliad 4.440, 15.119). 'Teucris', dative with 'immisit', 'sent in upon'. No elisions.

sentences.t:
Undique conveniunt, quoniam data copia pugnae
bellatorque animo deus incidit.
sentences.l:
From all sides they come together, since given was the chance of fighting
and the warrior god upon their spirits fell.
sentences.i: They gathered from every side, now that the chance to fight had been given them and the warrior god had come down upon their spirits.
sentences.n: 'conveniunt', the subject is the Latins. 'data (est) copia pugnae', 'the opportunity of battle has been given', the auxiliary left out, as often. 'bellator… deus', 'the warrior god', Mars; 'bellator', 'warrior', used as an adjective. 'animo incidit', 'fell upon their spirit', the god entering them, 'animo' a dative with the compound verb. Line 721 is a half-line, one of those Virgil left unfinished at his death; the poem keeps them as they are. Elision 'bellatorqu(e) animo'.

sentences.t:
Pandarus ut fuso germanum corpore cernit
et quo sit fortuna loco, qui casus agat res,
portam vi magna converso cardine torquet,
obnixus latis umeris, multosque suorum
moenibus exclusos duro in certamine linquit;
sentences.l:
Pandarus, when, his body poured out, his brother he sees,
and in what place fortune stands, what chance is driving things,
the gate with great force, its hinge turned, he twists,
shoving with his broad shoulders, and many of his own
shut out from the walls in the hard struggle he leaves;
sentences.i: When Pandarus saw his brother's body stretched on the ground, and understood how fortune stood and what turn events were taking, he heaved the gate round on its pivot with all his strength, pushing with his broad shoulders, and left many of his own men shut outside the walls in the bitter fighting;
sentences.n: 'ut… cernit', 'when he sees', 'ut' with the indicative meaning 'when'. 'fuso… corpore', ablative absolute, 'the body having been poured out', laid full length; 'germanum', 'his brother', Bitias. 'quo sit fortuna loco', 'in what position fortune is', and 'qui casus agat res', 'what chance drives events', indirect questions in the subjunctive. 'converso cardine', 'the hinge having been turned': an ancient door turned on a pivot, the 'cardo', set in sockets above and below. 'torquet', 'twists', the gate swinging heavily shut. 'obnixus', 'pushing hard against it', from 'obnitor'. 'multos… suorum', 'many of his own men', partitive genitive. Elision 'dur(o) in'.

sentences.t:
ast alios secum includit recipitque ruentis,
demens, qui Rutulum in medio non agmine regem
viderit inrumpentem ultroque incluserit urbi,
immanem veluti pecora inter inertia tigrim.
sentences.l:
but others with himself he shuts in, and receives them rushing,
the madman, who the Rutulian in the middle not of the column, the king,
had seen bursting in, and of his own accord shut him into the city,
a monstrous one, like a tiger among the sluggish flocks.
sentences.i: but others he shut in with himself and took them in as they came rushing back — the fool, who had not seen the Rutulian king bursting in among the throng and had actually shut him inside the town himself, a monstrous tiger among the helpless cattle.
sentences.n: 'ast', an old form of 'at', 'but'. 'ruentis', 'rushing', accusative plural in '-is'. 'demens', 'madman', Virgil's own comment on him. 'qui… non… viderit… incluserit', a relative clause of cause in the subjunctive, 'since he had not seen… and had shut in'; 'non' belongs to 'viderit'. 'Rutulum… regem', 'the Rutulian king', framing 'in medio… agmine', 'in the midst of the column'. 'ultro', 'of his own accord', going beyond what anyone could expect: he does the enemy's work for him. 'urbi', dative, 'in the city', the camp. 'immanem… tigrim', 'a monstrous tiger', framing the simile, which is packed into a single line; 'inter' stands between its adjective and noun. Elisions 'sec(um) includit', 'Rutul(um) in', 'inrumpent(em) ultroque', 'ultroqu(e) incluserit', 'pecor(a) inter'.

sentences.t:
Continuo nova lux oculis effulsit, et arma
horrendum sonuere; tremunt in vertice cristae
sanguineae, clipeoque micantia fulmina mittit:
sentences.l:
At once a strange light from his eyes flashed out, and his arms
terribly sounded; tremble on his crown the crests,
blood-red, and from his shield flashing lightnings he sends:
sentences.i: At once a strange light blazed from his eyes and his armour rang terribly; the blood-red crest quivered on the top of his helmet, and he flashed lightnings from his shield:
sentences.n: Everything here is Turnus's (his eyes, his armour, his crest), though only 'mittit' has him as its subject. 'Continuo', 'immediately'. 'nova lux', 'a new light', unearthly; 'oculis', 'from his eyes'. Homer gives Achilles' eyes a blaze like fire (Iliad 19.365–366) and makes fire play about the helmet and shield of Diomedes (Iliad 5.4–7). 'horrendum', a neuter adjective used as an adverb, 'dreadfully', as at 632. 'sonuere' = 'sonuerunt', the perfect in '-ere' (you'll see this constantly). 'in vertice', 'on the top', of the helmet; 'cristae sanguineae', 'the blood-red crests', the plume, held over to the next line. 'micantia fulmina', 'flashing thunderbolts', the gleam of the shield in the sun. No elisions.

sentences.t:
agnoscunt faciem invisam atque immania membra
turbati subito Aeneadae.
sentences.l:
recognise the hated face and the monstrous limbs,
thrown into confusion suddenly, the sons of Aeneas.
sentences.i: In sudden alarm the Aeneadae knew that hated face and those huge limbs.
sentences.n: 'agnoscunt', 'they recognise': the Trojans have seen Turnus before the walls since the start of the book. 'faciem invisam', 'the hated face'. 'immania membra', 'the huge limbs', the same words used of Bitias at 708. 'turbati', 'thrown into confusion', and the subject 'Aeneadae', 'the followers of Aeneas', a patronymic used for his people, both held back to the next line. 'Aeneadae' has four syllables, the first 'Ae-'. Elisions 'faci(em) invisam', 'invis(am) atque', 'atqu(e) immania', 'subit(o) Aeneadae'.

sentences.t:
Tum Pandarus ingens
emicat et mortis fraternae fervidus ira
effatur:
sentences.l:
Then Pandarus, huge,
springs forward, and with anger at his brother's death blazing
speaks out:
sentences.i: Then the giant Pandarus sprang forward and, hot with anger at his brother's death, called out:
sentences.n: 'ingens', 'huge', held to the end of the line: Pandarus is a giant like his brother. 'emicat', 'darts forward', leaps out. 'mortis fraternae… ira', 'anger at his brother's death', the genitive giving the cause of the anger; 'fraternae', 'of a brother', an adjective doing the work of a genitive. 'fervidus', 'glowing', boiling over. 'effatur', 'speaks out', the deponent 'effor', held over to the start of the next line before the speech begins. No elisions.

sentences.t:
“Non haec dotalis regia Amatae,
nec muris cohibet patriis media Ardea Turnum.
sentences.l:
“Not this is the dowry palace of Amata,
nor within his father's walls does Ardea, in its midst, hold Turnus.
sentences.i: “This is not the palace of Amata, promised to you as a dowry, nor is it Ardea, holding Turnus safe in the heart of his father's walls.
sentences.n: A speech begins. 'Non haec (est)', 'this is not', the verb left out. 'dotalis regia Amatae', 'the dowry palace of Amata': Queen Amata, wife of Latinus, wants Turnus for her daughter Lavinia, and with the bride would come the kingdom. 'muris… patriis', 'by his ancestral walls', framing 'cohibet', 'holds, encloses'. 'media Ardea', 'Ardea in the middle', with Turnus at its heart; Ardea is the Rutulian capital, Turnus's own city. Elisions 'regi(a) Amatae', 'medi(a) Ardea'.

sentences.t: Castra inimica vides; nulla hinc exire potestas.”
sentences.l: A hostile camp you see; there is no power to go out from here.”
sentences.i: It is an enemy camp you see around you; there is no way out of here.”
sentences.n: 'Castra inimica', 'an enemy camp', thrown to the front. 'nulla… potestas (est)', 'there is no possibility', the verb left out again; 'hinc exire', 'to go out from here', the infinitive with 'potestas'. Pandarus means the gate he has just shut: Turnus is trapped. The speech ends. Elisions 'Castr(a) inimica', 'null(a) hinc'.

sentences.t: Olli subridens sedato pectore Turnus:
sentences.l: To him, smiling, with calm breast, Turnus:
sentences.i: Turnus smiled at him, and answered with an untroubled heart:
sentences.n: 'Olli' = 'illi', 'to him', an archaic dative form; Jupiter smiles at Venus with the same two words at 1.254 ('Olli subridens'). 'sedato pectore', 'with a settled breast', ablative of manner: Turnus is calm where Pandarus is boiling. The verb of speaking is left out, as often ('Aeolus haec contra'). No elisions.

sentences.t: “Incipe, siqua animo virtus, et consere dextram:
sentences.l: “Begin, if any courage is in your spirit, and join your right hand:
sentences.i: “Come on, then, if you have any courage in you, and fight me hand to hand:
sentences.n: A speech begins. 'Incipe', 'begin', start the fight. 'siqua', Greenough's single word for 'si qua', 'if any', 'qua' the indefinite after 'si'; 'animo', 'in your spirit', with 'est' left out. 'consere dextram', 'join right hands', the old phrase for coming to close quarters, as 'conserere manum' or 'proelium'. Elision 'siqu(a) animo'.

sentences.t: hic etiam inventum Priamo narrabis Achillem.”
sentences.l: here too found for Priam you will tell an Achilles.”
sentences.i: you shall tell Priam that here, too, an Achilles has been found.”
sentences.n: 'narrabis', 'you will report', among the dead: Pandarus will meet Priam in the underworld. It turns round what Pyrrhus, Achilles' son, says to Priam just before he kills him, that Priam will carry the news to Achilles (2.547–549). 'inventum (esse)… Achillem', 'that an Achilles has been found', the accusative and infinitive with 'esse' left out. The Sibyl had warned Aeneas of 'another Achilles' born in Latium (6.89); Turnus claims the name. 'hic etiam', 'here too', in Italy as at Troy. The speech ends. Elision 'eti(am) inventum'.

sentences.t: Dixerat.
sentences.l: He had spoken.
sentences.i: He had spoken.
sentences.n: 'Dixerat', 'he had spoken', the pluperfect: a common way of closing a speech in Virgil before the action moves on. Here the speaker is Turnus, and the next sentence turns to Pandarus ('Ille'). No elisions.

sentences.t:
Ille rudem nodis et cortice crudo
intorquet summis adnixus viribus hastam:
sentences.l:
The other, rough with knots and with bark raw,
hurls, straining with his utmost strength, a spear:
sentences.i: Pandarus, straining with all his might, hurled a spear still rough with knots and raw bark:
sentences.n: 'Ille', 'he', the other man, Pandarus. 'rudem… hastam', 'a rough spear', framing the two lines: a shaft not smoothed, 'nodis et cortice crudo', 'with knots and untrimmed bark', ablatives with the adjective 'rudem', 'rough with'. 'intorquet', 'hurls with a twist', sends it spinning. 'adnixus', 'straining', from 'adnitor', Greenough's 'adn-' for 'ann-'. 'summis… viribus', 'with his utmost strength'. No elisions.

sentences.t: excepere aurae volnus;
sentences.l: received the breezes the wound;
sentences.i: the winds took the blow;
sentences.n: 'excepere' = 'exceperunt', 'caught', the '-ere' perfect. 'volnus', 'the wound', here the weapon that would have made it, a vivid use; Greenough's spelling of 'vulnus'. The spear goes harmlessly into the air. Elision 'exceper(e) aurae'.

sentences.t:
Saturnia Iuno
detorsit veniens, portaeque infigitur hasta.
sentences.l:
Saturnian Juno
turned it aside as it came, and in the gate is fixed the spear.
sentences.i: Saturnian Juno turned it aside in its flight, and the spear stuck fast in the gate.
sentences.n: 'Saturnia Iuno', 'Juno, daughter of Saturn', Turnus's protector throughout. 'detorsit', 'twisted away', deflected. 'veniens', 'coming', is best taken as a neuter accusative agreeing with 'volnus', the object understood: 'turned it aside as it came' (some take it with Juno, 'coming to help'). 'portae… infigitur', 'is fixed in the gate', 'portae' dative with the compound verb; 'hasta' is held to the end. The spear stops in the gate Pandarus has just shut. Elision 'portaequ(e) infigitur'.

sentences.t:
“At non hoc telum, mea quod vi dextera versat,
effugies;
sentences.l:
“But not this weapon, which my right hand with force wields,
will you escape;
sentences.i: “But this weapon, which my own right hand drives with all its strength, you will not escape;
sentences.n: A speech begins: Turnus answers at once, with no verb of speaking to introduce him; the opening mark and 'Sic ait' (749) tell you who is talking. 'At', 'but', the retort. 'hoc telum', 'this weapon', his sword. 'mea quod vi dextera versat', 'which my right hand wields with force', 'quod' put after 'mea', a common displacement in verse. 'versat', 'turns', brandishes. 'effugies', 'you will escape', held over to the next line, after the 'non' it belongs to. No elisions.

sentences.t: neque enim is teli nec volneris auctor.”
sentences.l: for not such is of weapon or of wound the author.”
sentences.i: the hand that deals this weapon and this wound is not like yours.”
sentences.n: 'neque enim', 'for… not'. 'is', 'such a man', a man of the kind you are; the sense is 'the author of this blow is no Pandarus'. 'teli… volneris auctor', 'the source of the weapon and the wound', the man behind them; 'volneris', Greenough's spelling of 'vulneris'. The speech ends. Elisions 'nequ(e) enim', 'en(im) is'.

sentences.t:
Sic ait et sublatum alte consurgit in ensem
et mediam ferro gemina inter tempora frontem
dividit inpubesque immani volnere malas.
sentences.l:
Thus he spoke, and, raised high, rises up into the sword,
and the forehead in the middle with the steel, between the twin temples,
he splits, and the beardless, with a monstrous wound, cheeks.
sentences.i: So he spoke, and rose to his full height into the blow of his lifted sword; the steel split Pandarus's forehead down the middle between the two temples, and his beardless cheeks, with a hideous wound.
sentences.n: 'Sic ait', 'thus he speaks'. 'sublatum alte consurgit in ensem', 'he rises up into his sword raised high', the whole body going into the downward stroke. 'mediam… frontem', 'the forehead in the middle', framing 'ferro gemina inter tempora', 'with the steel, between the twin temples'. 'dividit', 'splits', held to the start of the line. 'inpubes… malas', 'his beardless cheeks', accusative plural of 'impubes', Greenough's spelling with 'inp-': Pandarus is a young man for all his size. 'immani volnere', 'with a monstrous wound', framed by 'inpubes… malas'. Elisions 'sublat(um) alte', 'gemin(a) inter', 'inpubesqu(e) immani'.

sentences.t: Fit sonus, ingenti concussa est pondere tellus:
sentences.l: There is a crash; by the huge weight was shaken the earth:
sentences.i: There was a crash, and the earth shook under the enormous weight:
sentences.n: 'Fit sonus', 'a sound comes about', a crash as he falls. 'ingenti… pondere', 'by the huge weight', of the giant's body, framing 'concussa est', 'was shaken'; 'tellus', 'the earth', held to the end. 'concussa est' is pronounced as one word, 'concussast', the 'e' of 'est' dropping out after a vowel (prodelision). Homer marks a warrior's fall with a thud and the clang of his armour; here the ground itself shakes, as it groaned for Bitias (709). No elisions apart from 'concussa (e)st'.

sentences.t:
conlapsos artus atque arma cruenta cerebro
sternit humi moriens, atque illi partibus aequis
huc caput atque illuc umero ex utroque pependit.
sentences.l:
his collapsed limbs and his arms bloody with brain
he lays on the ground, dying, and to him in parts equal
this way his head and that way, from either shoulder, hung.
sentences.i: dying, he stretched his fallen limbs on the ground and his armour stained with his brain; and his head hung in two equal halves, this way and that, over either shoulder.
sentences.n: 'conlapsos artus', 'his collapsed limbs', Greenough's 'conl-' for 'coll-'. 'arma cruenta cerebro', 'arms bloody with brain', 'cerebro' ablative of means. 'sternit humi moriens', 'he lays (them) on the ground, dying': the dying man is the subject, as if he spread out his own body; 'humi', 'on the ground', the locative. 'illi', 'to him', a dative of reference where English says 'his'. 'partibus aequis', 'in equal parts', ablative of manner. 'huc… atque illuc', 'this way and that'. 'umero ex utroque', 'from each shoulder', with 'ex' after its noun. 'pependit', perfect of 'pendeo', 'hung'. Elisions 'atqu(e) arma', 'atqu(e) illi', 'atqu(e) illuc', 'umer(o) ex'.

sentences.t: Diffugiunt versi trepida formidine Troes:
sentences.l: Scatter, turned, in quaking fear, the Trojans:
sentences.i: The Trojans turned and scattered in panic:
sentences.n: 'Diffugiunt', 'they flee in different directions', 'dis-' meaning 'apart'. 'versi', 'turned', turned to flight. 'trepida formidine', 'with trembling fear', ablative of manner or cause. 'Troes', the Greek nominative plural of 'Tros', two syllables, 'Tro-es', held back to the end of the line. No elisions.

sentences.i: and if the victor had at once thought of breaking the bars by force and letting his comrades in at the gates, that day would have been the last of the war and of the Trojan nation;
sentences.n: A past condition contrary to fact: 'si… subisset… fuisset', pluperfect subjunctives, 'if (the thought) had come… (that day) would have been'. 'victorem', 'the victor', Turnus, the object of 'subisset', 'had come into (the mind of)'. 'ea cura', 'that concern', spelled out by the infinitives 'rumpere… immittere', 'to break… to let in'. 'claustra', 'the bars', the bolts of the gate. 'portis', ablative of the way, 'by the gates'. 'ultimus ille dies', 'that last day', 'bello gentique', datives, 'for the war and for the nation'. Virgil steps in to tell what did not happen. Elisions 'victor(em) ea', 'sociosqu(e) immittere'.

sentences.t:
sed furor ardentem caedisque insana cupido
egit in adversos.
sentences.l:
but fury the blazing man, and of slaughter mad desire,
drove against those facing him.
sentences.i: but fury and a mad lust for slaughter drove him on, blazing, against the men in front of him.
sentences.n: 'sed', 'but', the real course of events. 'furor… caedisque insana cupido', 'fury and mad desire', two subjects with a singular verb, 'egit'. 'ardentem', 'him burning', Turnus, the object. 'caedis', 'of slaughter', objective genitive with 'cupido', 'desire', here feminine, as in prose. 'in adversos', 'against those facing (him)', the men in his way, not the gate behind him. Line 761 is a half-line, like 721, left unfinished by Virgil. Elision 'caedisqu(e) insana'.

sentences.t:
Principio Phalerim et succiso poplite Gygen
excipit;
sentences.l:
First Phaleris, and, his knee-tendon cut, Gyges
he catches;
sentences.i: First he caught Phaleris, and Gyges, hamstringing him;
sentences.n: 'Principio', 'first', beginning a list of kills. 'Phalerim', 'Gygen', Greek accusatives of Phaleris and Gyges. 'succiso poplite', ablative absolute, 'the back of the knee having been cut', the hamstring severed so that the man falls. 'excipit', 'catches', 'takes', of meeting and bringing down an enemy, held over to the next line. Elision 'Phaler(im) et'.

sentences.t:
hinc raptas fugientibus ingerit hastas
in tergum, Iuno vires animumque ministrat;
sentences.l:
then spears snatched up at the fleeing he hurls
into the back; Juno strength and spirit supplies;
sentences.i: then he picked up the spears and flung them into the backs of the fleeing men; Juno supplied him with strength and spirit;
sentences.n: 'hinc', 'next'. 'raptas… hastas', 'spears snatched up', framing the line; Turnus takes the weapons he finds on the ground and uses them on the Trojans as they run. 'fugientibus', 'at the fleeing', dative with 'ingerit', 'heaps on', hurls at; 'in tergum', 'into the back'. 'Iuno… ministrat', set beside the killing without a connective (asyndeton): Juno gives Turnus what Mars gave the Latins at 717, 'vires animumque', 'strength and spirit'. No elisions.

sentences.t:
addit Halym comitem et confixa Phegea parma,
ignaros deinde in muris Martemque cientis
Alcandrumque Haliumque Noemonaque Prytanimque.
sentences.i: he added Halys, his comrade, and Phegeus, whose shield he pierced, and then men on the walls who were rousing the battle and did not know he was there, Alcander and Halius, Noemon and Prytanis.
sentences.n: 'addit', 'he adds', to the dead. 'Halym', 'Phegea', 'Noemona', Greek accusatives of Halys, Phegeus and Noemon. 'comitem', 'companion', of Phegeus or of the others. 'confixa… parma', ablative absolute, 'his small shield having been pierced'. 'ignaros', 'unaware' that Turnus is inside. 'Martem… cientis', 'rousing Mars', stirring up battle, 'Mars' standing for war; 'cientis' accusative plural in '-is'. 'deinde', two syllables; 'Noemona' four, No-e-mo-na, and the '-que' before 'Prytanim' is long, as Homer's 'te' is before 'Prytanin'. Line 767, all names and '-que', copies a line of Homer that lists men killed by Odysseus (Iliad 5.678): 'Alkandron th' Halion te Noemona te Prytanin te'. Elisions 'comit(em) et', 'deind(e) in', 'Alcandrumqu(e) Haliumque'.

sentences.i: Lynceus was coming at him, calling to his comrades, but Turnus struck first, lunging with his flashing sword from the rampart on his right;
sentences.n: 'Lyncea', the Greek accusative of Lynceus, three syllables, Lyn-ce-a. 'tendentem contra', 'pushing against him', coming to meet him. 'vibranti gladio', 'with a quivering sword', brandished so that it flashes. 'conixus', 'straining', from 'conitor'. 'ab aggere', 'from the rampart', the earthwork inside the walls. 'dexter', probably 'on the right' (some take it 'with his right hand'), an adjective doing the work of an adverb. 'occupat', 'seizes first', gets his blow in before the other's: the subject is Turnus, held back to the start of the line. No elisions.

sentences.t:
huic uno desectum comminus ictu
cum galea longe iacuit caput.
sentences.l:
for him, with one, cut off, close at hand, stroke,
with the helmet far off lay his head.
sentences.i: with a single stroke at close quarters his head was cut off and lay far away, helmet and all.
sentences.n: 'huic', 'to him', a dative of reference: 'his head'. 'uno… ictu', 'with a single stroke', framing 'desectum comminus', 'cut off at close range'. 'cum galea', 'with the helmet', still on. 'longe iacuit', 'lay far off'; 'iacuit' begins with a consonantal i, 'yacuit'. 'caput', 'head', saved for the end. No elisions.

sentences.t:
Inde ferarum
vastatorem Amycum, quo non felicior alter
ungere tela manu ferrumque armare veneno,
sentences.l:
Then of wild beasts
the ravager Amycus, than whom no other more successful
to anoint weapons by hand and to arm the steel with poison,
sentences.i: Next he killed Amycus, the destroyer of wild beasts, whom no one surpassed in smearing weapons and arming steel with poison,
sentences.n: The list runs on with no new verb: understand 'he kills' from what precedes. 'ferarum vastatorem', 'the ravager of wild beasts', a hunter. 'quo non felicior alter', 'than whom no other (was) more fortunate', 'quo' ablative of comparison; 'felicior', 'more successful', with the infinitives 'ungere… armare', 'at anointing… at arming'. The turn of phrase is the one Virgil used for the trumpeter Misenus, 'quo non praestantior alter / aere ciere viros' (6.164–165). 'manu', 'by hand'. 'veneno', 'with poison', for his hunting weapons. Elisions 'vastator(em) Amycum', 'ferrumqu(e) armare'.

sentences.t:
et Clytium Aeoliden et amicum Crethea Musis,
Crethea Musarum comitem, cui carmina semper
et citharae cordi numerosque intendere nervis.
[Semper equos atque arma virum pugnasque canebat.]
sentences.l:
and Clytius, son of Aeolus, and the friend Cretheus of the Muses,
Cretheus, the Muses' companion, to whom songs always
and lyres were a delight, and rhythms to stretch upon strings.
[Always horses and arms of men and battles he sang.]
sentences.i: and Clytius, son of Aeolus, and Cretheus, the friend of the Muses — Cretheus, the Muses' companion, whose heart was always in songs and the lyre and in setting measures to its strings. [Always it was horses and the arms of men and battles that he sang.]
sentences.n: 'Aeoliden', 'son of Aeolus', a Greek patronymic in the accusative, used of Misenus at 6.164. 'Crethea', the Greek accusative of Cretheus, repeated at the head of the next line (epanalepsis), a sign of pity. 'cui… cordi', 'to whom… (were) dear to the heart', a double dative ('cordi est', 'it is dear'): 'carmina', 'citharae' and the infinitive 'intendere' are the subjects. 'numeros… intendere nervis', 'to stretch rhythms on the strings', to set music to the lyre. Line 777 is bracketed by Greenough as spurious and is kept here inside [ ]: it is generally taken to be a later addition. 'virum' = 'virorum'. 'arma virum' recalls the poem's first words. Elisions 'Clyti(um) Aeoliden', 'numerosqu(e) intendere', 'atqu(e) arma'.

sentences.t:
Tandem ductores audita caede suorum
conveniunt Teucri, Mnestheus acerque Serestus,
palantisque vident socios hostemque receptum.
sentences.l:
At last the leaders, having heard of the slaughter of their own,
come together, of the Teucrians, Mnestheus and keen Serestus,
and straggling they see their comrades, and the enemy let in.
sentences.i: At last the Trojan leaders, Mnestheus and fierce Serestus, heard of the slaughter of their men and came together, and saw their comrades scattering and the enemy inside the walls.
sentences.n: A new paragraph in Greenough. 'audita caede suorum', ablative absolute, 'the slaughter of their own men having been heard of'. 'ductores… Teucri', 'the Trojan leaders', 'Teucri' here an adjective; 'eu' is one syllable, as in 'Mnestheus'. Mnestheus and Serestus were the two captains Aeneas left in charge of the camp (171–173). 'palantis… socios', 'their comrades straggling', 'palantis' accusative plural in '-is', from 'palor', 'wander'. 'hostem… receptum', 'the enemy received', let in through their own gate. No elisions.

sentences.t: Et Mnestheus: “Quo deinde fugam, quo tenditis? ”inquit.
sentences.l: And Mnestheus: “Where next your flight, where are you directing?” he says.
sentences.i: And Mnestheus cried, “Where are you running now? Where are you heading?”
sentences.n: The print has 'tenditis? ”inquit', a misprint for 'tenditis?” inquit', corrected here: the closing mark is joined to the next word (as at 423); t keeps the print. 'Et Mnestheus', 'and Mnestheus (says)', the verb of speaking left out and then supplied by 'inquit' after the first question. 'Quo deinde', 'where next?'; 'deinde' is two syllables. 'fugam… tenditis', 'are you directing your flight', with 'quo… quo' repeated in reproach. No elisions.

sentences.t: “Quos alios muros, quae iam ultra moenia habetis?
sentences.l: “What other walls, what further now fortifications do you have?
sentences.i: “What other walls, what defences have you left beyond these?
sentences.n: The speech resumes after 'inquit', with a new opening mark. 'Quos alios muros', 'what other walls', the indignant question: the camp is their last refuge in Italy. 'quae… moenia', 'what fortifications', 'ultra', 'further', 'beyond (these)'; 'iam', 'now', when this one is lost. Elisions 'i(am) ultra', 'moeni(a) habetis'.

sentences.t:
Unus homo et vestris, o cives, undique saeptus
aggeribus tantas strages inpune per urbem
ediderit, iuvenum primos tot miserit Orco?
sentences.l:
One man, and by your, o citizens, on every side hemmed in
ramparts, such great slaughter with impunity through the city
shall he have made, of the young men the foremost so many sent to Orcus?
sentences.i: Is one man, citizens, hemmed in on every side by your own ramparts, to have spread such carnage through the town unpunished, and sent so many of our best young men down to Orcus?
sentences.n: 'Unus homo… ediderit… miserit', a question of indignation in the perfect subjunctive, 'is one man to have made… sent?'. 'vestris… aggeribus', 'by your ramparts', framing 'o cives, undique saeptus', 'citizens, fenced in on every side': Turnus is the one inside the walls now, and still they run. 'tantas strages', 'such great carnage', 'strages' accusative plural. 'inpune', Greenough's spelling of 'impune', 'unpunished'. 'iuvenum primos', 'the first of the young men', the best of them. 'Orco', 'to Orcus', god of the dead and so the underworld, a dative of direction. Elision 'hom(o) et'.

sentences.t:
Non infelicis patriae veterumque deorum
et magni Aeneae, segnes, miseretque pudetque?”
sentences.l:
Not of your unhappy fatherland and your ancient gods
and of great Aeneas, sluggards, do you feel pity and shame?”
sentences.i: Have you no pity, you laggards, and no shame, for your unhappy country, for your ancient gods, for great Aeneas?”
sentences.n: 'miseret… pudet', impersonal verbs, 'it moves to pity… it shames', with the genitive of what causes the feeling ('patriae… deorum… Aeneae') and the person feeling it in the accusative, here understood ('vos'). 'Non… ', a question expecting 'yes', 'are you not moved?'. 'infelicis patriae', 'your unhappy country', Troy, now this camp. 'veterum… deorum', 'your ancient gods', the Penates brought from Troy. 'segnes', 'sluggish ones', a vocative of reproach. 'miseretque pudetque', the double '-que… -que', 'both… and'. The speech ends. Elision 'magn(i) Aeneae'.

sentences.t:
Talibus accensi firmantur et agmine denso
consistunt.
sentences.l:
By such things fired, they are steadied, and in a column dense
they stand firm.
sentences.i: Fired by such words, they took heart, and formed up in a close-packed line.
sentences.n: 'Talibus', 'by such (words)', 'dictis' understood. 'accensi', 'kindled'. 'firmantur', 'are made firm', recover their nerve. 'agmine denso', 'in a dense column', ablative of manner. 'consistunt', 'they halt and stand', stop running and hold their ground, held over to the start of the next line. No elisions.

sentences.t:
Turnus paulatim excedere pugna
et fluvium petere ac partem, quae cingitur unda;
sentences.l:
Turnus, little by little, began to withdraw from the fight
and to make for the river and the part which is encircled by the water;
sentences.i: Turnus, little by little, began to give ground from the fight and make for the river and the side of the camp that the water surrounds;
sentences.n: 'excedere… petere', historic infinitives: the infinitive standing for the main verb in a lively narrative, 'Turnus began to withdraw… make for'. 'pugna', 'from the fight', ablative of separation. 'fluvium', 'the river', the Tiber, which bordered one side of the Trojan camp. 'partem, quae cingitur unda', 'the part which is encircled by the water', the riverside of the camp. Elisions 'paulat(im) excedere', 'peter(e) ac'.

sentences.t:
acrius hoc Teucri clamore incumbere magno
et glomerare manum.
sentences.l:
the more keenly for this did the Teucrians, with shouting, press on, great,
and gather their band.
sentences.i: all the more fiercely the Trojans pressed on with a great shout and massed their numbers.
sentences.n: 'acrius hoc', 'the more keenly by this', 'hoc' ablative of the degree of difference: the more he gives way, the harder they push. 'incumbere… glomerare', two more historic infinitives. 'clamore… magno', 'with a great shout', framing 'incumbere', 'to lean upon', press on. 'glomerare manum', 'to mass their band', draw together in a body. Elision 'clamor(e) incumbere'.

sentences.t:
Ceu saevum turba leonem
cum telis premit infensis, at territus ille,
asper, acerba tuens, retro redit, et neque terga
ira dare aut virtus patitur, nec tendere contra
ille quidem hoc cupiens potis est per tela virosque:
sentences.l:
As when a fierce lion a crowd
with weapons presses, hostile, but he, frightened,
savage, glaring bitterly, backwards goes, and neither his back
anger to give nor courage allows, nor to press against them
is he, indeed wishing this, able, through weapons and men:
sentences.i: As when a throng of men bears hard with hostile weapons on a savage lion, and he, shaken yet still fierce, with a baleful glare, gives ground slowly; anger and courage forbid him to turn tail, yet, much as he longs to, he cannot drive at them through the spears and the men:
sentences.n: The model is Homer's Ajax giving ground before the Trojans like a lion driven from the cattle-yard (Iliad 11.548–555). 'Ceu… cum', 'as when'. 'saevum… leonem', 'a fierce lion', framing 'turba', 'a crowd'. 'telis… infensis', 'with hostile weapons'. 'asper', 'savage'. 'acerba tuens', 'glaring bitterly', 'acerba' a neuter plural used as an adverb. 'retro redit', 'goes back backwards', retreats. 'neque… patitur', 'neither… allows', singular with the nearer subject; 'terga dare', 'to give his back', to run. 'potis est' = 'potest', 'is able', an old form. 'ille quidem hoc cupiens', 'though he wants it'. Elisions 'dar(e) aut', 'quid(em) hoc'.

sentences.t:
haud aliter retro dubius vestigia Turnus
improperata refert, et mens exaestuat ira.
sentences.l:
not otherwise backwards, wavering, his steps Turnus
unhurried takes back, and his mind boils with anger.
sentences.i: even so Turnus, in two minds, gave back, step by unhurried step, his heart seething with anger.
sentences.n: 'haud aliter', 'not otherwise', closing the simile. 'dubius', 'uncertain', torn between retreat and attack, like the lion. 'vestigia… improperata refert', 'brings back unhastened steps', 'refert' from 're-' + 'fero'; 'improperata', 'not hurried', a rare word, framing with 'vestigia' the name 'Turnus'. 'mens exaestuat ira', 'his mind boils over with anger', 'ira' ablative of cause; 'exaestuo', 'surge up', of the sea in a storm. No elisions.

sentences.t:
Quin etiam bis tum medios invaserat hostis,
bis confusa fuga per muros agmina vertit;
sentences.l:
Indeed, twice then into the midst had he charged of the enemy,
twice, confused in flight, along the walls the columns he turned;
sentences.i: What is more, twice even then he had charged into the thick of the enemy, and twice routed their ranks and sent them flying along the walls;
sentences.n: 'Quin etiam', 'indeed, even', adding more. 'bis… bis', 'twice… twice', one in each clause. 'invaserat', pluperfect, 'had charged into', 'medios… hostis', 'the midst of the enemy', 'hostis' accusative plural in '-is'. 'confusa fuga… agmina', 'the columns thrown into confusion by flight': the metre shows that 'fugā', 'in flight', is an ablative with a long final 'a', so 'confusa' goes with 'agmina'. 'per muros', 'along the walls'. 'vertit', 'turned', put to flight. No elisions.

sentences.t:
sed manus e castris propere coit omnis in unum,
nec contra vires audet Saturnia Iuno
sufficere, aëriam caelo nam Iuppiter Irim
demisit germanae haud mollia iussa ferentem,
ni Turnus cedat Teucrorum moenibus altis.
sentences.l:
but the band from the camp hastily gathers, all, into one,
nor against them strength dares Saturnian Juno
to supply; for airy, from heaven, Jupiter Iris
sent down to his sister, by no means gentle orders bearing,
if Turnus does not withdraw from the Teucrians' walls high.
sentences.i: but the whole Trojan force in the camp was quickly gathering in one body, and Saturnian Juno dared not supply him with strength against them, for Jupiter had sent Iris down through the air from heaven to his sister, bearing orders that were far from gentle should Turnus not withdraw from the Trojans' high walls.
sentences.n: 'manus… omnis', 'the whole band', framing 'e castris propere coit', 'quickly comes together from the camp'; 'in unum', 'into one (place)'. 'nec… audet… sufficere', 'nor does she dare to supply', 'vires', 'strength', with 'contra', 'against (them)'. 'aëriam… Irim', 'airy Iris', the messenger goddess of the rainbow, the diaeresis marking a-e as two syllables; 'nam' is set late in its clause. 'germanae', 'to his sister', Juno being both. 'haud mollia', 'not gentle', a litotes. 'ni Turnus cedat', 'if Turnus does not withdraw': the threat in Jupiter's orders, reported, with the 'or else' left out. The book opened with Juno sending Iris to Turnus (9.2). In Homer Zeus sends Iris to turn back Hera and Athena (Iliad 8.397–408). Elisions 'sufficer(e) aëriam', 'german(ae) haud'.

sentences.t:
Ergo nec clipeo iuvenis subsistere tantum
nec dextra valet:
sentences.l:
Therefore neither with his shield can the young man hold out so much
nor with his right hand:
sentences.i: And so the young warrior could no longer hold his ground as before, neither with his shield nor with his sword-hand:
sentences.n: 'Ergo', 'therefore', now that no goddess helps him. 'iuvenis', 'the young man', Turnus. 'nec… nec', 'neither… nor', with 'clipeo… dextra', 'with his shield… with his right hand', defence and attack. 'subsistere tantum', 'to hold firm so much', as much as he had; 'valet', 'is strong enough', held over with 'dextra' to the next line. 'iuvenis' begins with a consonantal i. No elisions.

sentences.t:
iniectis sic undique telis
obruitur.
sentences.l:
with missiles thrown in, so, from every side,
he is overwhelmed.
sentences.i: so thickly did the spears rain in on him from all sides that he was overwhelmed.
sentences.n: 'iniectis… telis', ablative absolute, 'missiles having been thrown in (at him)', framing 'sic undique', 'so, from all sides'; in 'iniectis' the i after the prefix is a consonant, 'in-yectis'. 'obruitur', 'he is buried', overwhelmed, held over to the start of 808. No elisions.

sentences.t:
Strepit adsiduo cava tempora circum
tinnitu galea, et saxis solida aera fatiscunt,
discussaeque iubae capiti, nec sufficit umbo
ictibus:
sentences.l:
Clangs with unceasing, the hollow temples round,
ringing the helmet, and with stones the solid bronze gapes open,
and struck away are the plumes from his head, nor is equal the boss
to the blows:
sentences.i: His helmet rang and rang about his hollow temples, the solid bronze cracked under the stones, the crest was knocked from his head, and the boss of his shield could not withstand the blows:
sentences.n: The model is Homer's Ajax at the ships, his helmet ringing under the blows, his shoulder tired from holding up the shield, his breath laboured, the sweat pouring off him (Iliad 16.102–111). 'Strepit… galea', 'the helmet clangs', 'adsiduo… tinnitu', 'with continual ringing', framing 'cava tempora circum', 'round his hollow temples', 'circum' after its noun. 'solida aera', 'the solid bronze', 'aera' neuter plural of 'aes'. 'fatiscunt', 'gape', split. 'discussae… iubae', 'the plumes (are) struck off', 'capiti', dative, 'from his head'. 'umbo', the boss, standing for the shield; 'sufficit… ictibus', 'is equal to the blows'. Elisions 'gale(a) et', 'solid(a) aera'.

sentences.t:
ingeminant hastis et Troes et ipse
fulmineus Mnestheus.
sentences.l:
they redouble with spears, both the Trojans and himself,
thunderbolt-like Mnestheus.
sentences.i: the Trojans showered spears on him again and again, and Mnestheus himself, like a thunderbolt.
sentences.n: 'ingeminant', 'they redouble', the blows. 'hastis', 'with spears'. 'et Troes et ipse… Mnestheus', 'both the Trojans and Mnestheus himself', 'Troes' two syllables, 'Mnestheus' with 'eu' as one. 'fulmineus', 'like the thunderbolt', 'of lightning', an epithet of a warrior's force. No elisions.

sentences.i: Then the sweat poured down all over his body, driving a stream black as pitch, and he had no chance to draw breath;
sentences.n: 'toto corpore', 'over his whole body', ablative of place. 'sudor liquitur', 'sweat flows', 'liquitur' from the deponent 'liquor', 'melt, run'. 'et piceum… flumen agit', 'and it drives a pitch-black stream', the sweat mixed with dust and blood, framing the parenthesis 'nec respirare potestas', 'nor is there any chance to breathe', 'est' left out. No elisions.

sentences.t: fessos quatit aeger anhelitus artus.
sentences.l: his weary shakes the sick panting limbs.
sentences.i: his gasping breath shook his weary limbs.
sentences.n: 'fessos… artus', 'his weary limbs', framing the clause. 'aeger anhelitus', 'sick panting', the laboured breath of exhaustion, the subject of 'quatit', 'shakes'. Homer's Ajax breathes hard in the same way (Iliad 16.109–110). No elisions.

sentences.t:
Tum demum praeceps saltu sese omnibus armis
in fluvium dedit:
sentences.l:
Then at last headlong with a leap himself with all his arms
into the river he gave:
sentences.i: Then at last, with a leap, he threw himself headlong into the river in full armour:
sentences.n: 'Tum demum', 'then at last', only when he can no more. 'praeceps', 'headlong'. 'saltu', 'with a leap'. 'sese… dedit', 'gave himself', flung himself; 'sese' the strengthened 'se'. 'omnibus armis', 'with all his arms', ablative of accompaniment without 'cum', as often with military words: he jumps in his armour. Elision 'ses(e) omnibus'.

sentences.t:
ille suo cum gurgite flavo
accepit venientem ac mollibus extulit undis
et laetum sociis abluta caede remisit.
sentences.l:
it, with its yellow flood,
received him coming and on gentle waves bore him up
and, glad, to his comrades, the slaughter washed off, sent him back.
sentences.i: the river, with its yellow flood, received him as he came, held him up on gentle waves, and sent him back glad to his comrades, the slaughter rinsed away.
sentences.n: 'ille', 'it', the river, the Tiber, now the subject. 'suo cum gurgite flavo', 'with its yellow flood', 'flavus' being the Tiber's standing colour (7.31). 'venientem', 'him coming'. 'mollibus… undis', 'on gentle waves'. 'extulit', 'bore up'. 'laetum', 'glad', Turnus. 'abluta caede', ablative absolute, 'the slaughter having been washed off', the blood of his victims. 'remisit', 'sent back'. Book IX ends here, with Turnus safe; in Book VIII the river god had shown himself to Aeneas as his helper (8.62–64). Elision 'venient(em) ac'.
